t: a branch. A group of threads that hang down from the garment like a branch from a tree.
the corner of the garment. The corner of the garment.
of the same material as the garment. From the material from which the garment is made (as explained below 3:5).
like the tzitzit of the head. The hair of the head.
a number by Torah law. But by rabbinic law it has a number, as explained below, halachah 6.
like the sky. The color of the sky.
and winds it around the branch. Wraps it around the other threads in the branch.
a measure by Torah law. And see below, halachah 6, how it is practiced.
two commandments. Two directives.
"and they shall make for themselves tzitzit". A directive to make the branch of tzitzit.
"and they shall put on the tzitzit of the corner a thread of tekhelet". A directive to wind the tekhelet.
does not prevent. One can fulfill the one commandment without fulfilling the other.
and the white was cut off and reduced up to the corner. The white threads were torn off entirely.
and the four tzitzit prevent one another. Only if he attached tzitzit to all four corners has he fulfilled the commandment.
from the corner. The corner of the garment.
from the knot of the thumb. The distance from the middle joint of the thumb to the tip of the nail.
and doubles them in the middle. So that the four threads hang from both sides of the garment.
and every finger-breadth is by the thumb. A finger-breadth is measured by the width of the thumb (and its measure is explained in Hilchot Sefer Torah 9:9).
and one of the eight threads shall be a thread of tekhelet. That he spins a single thread, part of which is tekhelet and part white (Responsa of Maimonides, 286).
for we ascend in holiness and do not descend. Since he begins with white, he ends with it, so as not to diminish its importance.

so that it be adjacent to the corner of its kind. So that next to the corner of the garment there be a thread of the same kind as the garment and in its color. But most of the windings are from the tekhelet thread.
no fewer than seven and no more than thirteen. Seven corresponds to the seven heavens, and thirteen corresponds to the seven heavens and the six spaces between them (Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 39a).
and the beauty of the tekhelet. The pleasing way of tying the tekhelet.
and he must unravel it until it is like the tzitzit of the hair of the head. He leaves the end of the branch without windings, so that the threads remain separated like the hairs of the head.
one who makes white without tekhelet. For the tekhelet does not prevent, as explained above, halachah 4. For example, one who has no tekhelet (see below 2:9).
twisted. Spun from several fine threads.
is counted only as one thread. Although the thread is twisted from eight separate threads, it is not counted as eight threads but as one.
for the sake of tzitzit. For the purpose of the commandment.
the hairs that are plucked from the animal. Hairs that were torn off and not sheared.

from the remnants of the warp that the weaver leaves at the end of the garment. A garment is made of lengthwise threads (called the warp) and crosswise threads (called the weft). Sometimes after weaving, the fringes of the lengthwise threads remain.
from the shearing. The wool that was sheared for spinning.
the condemned city. A city most of whose inhabitants are idol worshipers, all of whose property must be burned (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 4:6).
from consecrated property. From a sheep or wool belonging to the Temple treasury.
one who bows to an animal, its wool is invalid for tzitzit. Although the wool is not forbidden because of this (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:1), nevertheless one should not use it for a commandment.
for it has changed. When it was worshiped it was wood, and now threads have been made from it (compare Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:14).

and tzitzit that was made from what was made previously. That the attaching of the threads was done in a manner that is not effective for fulfilling the commandment of tzitzit, and only after the tzitzit was already tied did he correct the matter, as explained in the following halachot.
a corner that has tzitzit in it. A piece of garment to which tzitzit threads have already been attached.
he attached the threads, etc.. He attached threads to two corners of the same garment and tied each corner properly, and afterward cut the threads so that two valid tzitzit were formed.
intertwined with one another. Joined to one another.
he attached tzitzit on top of tzitzit. He tied tzitzit threads on a corner that already had threads.
if he intended to nullify the first. When he tied the second threads, his intention was to nullify the first threads.
when he added, he invalidated all. For a corner with two branches is invalid because of "do not add."
one who attaches to a garment of three. Corners, which is not obligated in tzitzit, as explained below 3:3.
and one attaches tzitzit to its four corners when it is folded. For if one were to unfold the folds, there would be two tzitzit in the middle of the garment.
if he sewed all of it. He sewed the entire fold so that the folding is fixed.
they fold. They fold over.
the corner was torn off. It was ripped and separated from the garment.
beyond three fingerbreadths. At a distance of three fingerbreadths or more from the edge of the garment.

within three, he may not sew. For the piece that was torn off is smaller than the minimum size of a corner (see above, halachah 6), and is no longer considered part of this garment, and when he sews it back it is as if he is attaching a new corner to the garment, which is like one that came about on its own (as explained above, halachah 13).

the corner of a garment was diminished. The corner of the garment began to tear so that the tzitzit threads are near the edge of the garment, even less than the width of a thumb-knot (see above, halachah 6).
enough for a loop. Sufficient length to make a loop from it.
from its base. At the place where it is attached to the garment, before the windings and knots.
the tekhelet mentioned in the Torah everywhere. Regarding the making of the Tabernacle and the priestly garments (see also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 8:13).
mixed. Blended.
of kohl. A blue dye used for women's jewelry. The color of tekhelet resembles the color of kohl mixed with white.
the likeness of the sky as seen by the eye. The color in which the sky appears to our eyes (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 3:3).
in the clarity of the sky. When the sky is clear.
and the tekhelet mentioned regarding tzitzit etc.. The tekhelet made for tzitzit is distinct in its method of preparation, so that its color will not change.
like the appearance of the sky. In the color of the heavens.
with isatis. A plant used for dyeing garments blue.
with other dark dyes. Those who dye with a dark color.
its wool is invalid for tzitzit. Its wool is not considered wool for the purpose of tzitzit (and in other contexts see Hilchot Kilayim 10:2, Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 13:3).
and soaks it in lime. To clean the wool and prepare it for dyeing.
with ahala. A plant used for laundering (see for example Hilchot Shemitah 5:10).
so that it will absorb the color. So that it will absorb the dye afterward.
its color. Its dye.
and in the Dead Sea. That is, the Mediterranean Sea (see Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 8:8 in accurate versions).
into a cauldron. A large pot in which the wool is dyed.
spices. Various materials useful for dyeing.
kimonya. A grass used for laundering (see for example Hilchot Shabbat 18:8).
for its sake. For the sake of the commandment of tzitzit.
the entire cauldron is disqualified. For the dye in it was used for testing and not for the sake of the commandment, and all the dye is disqualified because of that.
for he tested it and disqualified it. He tested wool dyeing with it, and thereby disqualified it.
the expert. One whose profession is dyeing wool for tzitzit and who is well versed in its laws.
that do not hold. Whose color does not last.
for a day and a night. For twenty-four hours.
in its color. In its hue.
and it did not fade. The dye did not become dull.
that they let rot for muries. They let it spoil to prepare a pickled-fish sauce.
unspecified. Without verification.
lest he replaced it. Because its price is high, he may come to replace it with counterfeit tekhelet.
sealed with two seals. Which ensure that the tekhelet was not replaced (for the manner of sealing see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 13:8).
cut off. Cut to the length of tzitzit strings.
invalid. Lest they were dyed and spun for another purpose.

and if twisted, it is valid. For their form proves that they were made for tzitzit (this is the reading in Responsa of the Rambam 287. Some read in this halachah: "cut off and twisted - invalid," and according to this version in any case we assume they were made for another purpose).
a garment with tzitzit. A garment to which tzitzit strings are tied.
from the merchant. The trader - valid, for by default he bought it from an Israelite (although by law one may not sell such a garment to a gentile, see below 3:9).
from a commoner. One who is not a merchant - invalid, since we do not assume that he acquired it from an Israelite.
his head and most of his body. His head and the majority of his body.
and he does not need another to watch him. He is old enough to walk in the marketplace alone.
wool. Sheep's wool.
linen. Flax.
and goat hair. The wool of goats.
square. With four corners.

garments mentioned in the Torah without specification etc.. Unspecified garments mentioned in the Torah are those made of wool or linen (see Hilchot Kelim 22:1). And regarding tzitzit it says: "and they shall make for themselves fringes on the corners of their garments" (Numbers 15:38).
for four are included within five. A garment with five corners includes four corners and one extra corner.
for it says, "on the four corners of your garment". Even if there are more than four corners, he attaches tzitzit only to four.
if it is of leather... it is exempt. For leather is not considered a garment at all, and it is exempt from tzitzit even by rabbinic law (unlike the materials mentioned above, halachah 2).
from there on it is obligated. Because it already looks like his own.
of its own kind. They make the strings from the same material from which the garment is made.
they exempt. One fulfills the obligation of tzitzit with them.
even though it is white alone. When he makes the tzitzit from white threads only.
by law. By the essential law.
for shaatnez is permitted with regard to tzitzit. The prohibition of shaatnez (wearing a garment made of wool and linen) is set aside for the commandment of tzitzit (see also Hilchot Kilayim 10:4).

and anywhere you find a positive commandment and a negative commandment. That contradict one another, such as here where the positive commandment of tzitzit contradicts the negative commandment of shaatnez (for this principle see Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 3:5).
not because tzitzit is set aside because of shaatnez. For it was explained in the previous halachah that shaatnez is permitted with regard to tzitzit.
violates a negative commandment. Of wearing shaatnez.
even on Shabbat. And it is even permitted to go out wearing this garment from one domain to another, for tzitzit are not considered a burden (Hilchot Shabbat 19:20).

and from when does he recite the blessing... from when he can distinguish between the tekhelet in it and the white in it. From the time there is enough light to distinguish between the tzitzit threads. [Note: In the Commentary on the Mishnah the Rambam vocalizes the word "me'eimatai" as "me'ammatai."]
and whenever. Each time.

for the end of the commandment. The fulfillment of the commandment is not in making the garment but in wrapping oneself in it, and therefore he recites the blessing then (see also Hilchot Berachot 11:8).
were torn off. Were ripped or pulled off.
a commandment whose body has no sanctity. No sanctity applies to the tzitzit themselves, as it does to tefillin or a Torah scroll (see Hilchot Sefer Torah 10:4).
lest he wrap himself in it. The gentile, and appear to be an Israelite (for this concern see Hilchot Rotze'ach 12:7).

in order to educate him in the commandments. To accustom him to the observance of the commandments (for further examples see Hilchot Kriat Shema 4:1, Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 6:10, Hilchot Shevitat Asor 2:10, Hilchot Sukkah 6:1 and others).
a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and whose sex is unclear. [Note: The Rambam in the Commentary on the Mishnah vocalizes this word "tumtom."]
and an androginos. One who has both male and female organs.

for it is not an obligation of the garment but an obligation of the man. There is no obligation that the garment have tzitzit; rather, the obligation is on the person who wears a garment to wear one with tzitzit.
and at the time of prayer one must be especially careful. Out of respect for prayer (see Hilchot Tefillah 5:5).
weighed it and hung all the commandments on it. The commandment of tzitzit is equal to all the commandments, and when one sees it one remembers the other commandments.
